title: Alas! by Nature How Depraved
description: Alas! by Nature How Depraved in Tonic Solfa to ST. AGNES, doh is G: the solfa with the words, staff notation, 7 verses and a piano.
about: John Newton wrote these words. They were printed in Olney Hymns (London, 1779), Book II, hymn 29, “How shall I put thee among the children? Jer 3:19”.
The book printed the words without tunes, marked Common Metre (8.6.8.6), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to ST. AGNES; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.
underlay: A-las! by na-ture how de-praved, How prone to ev-ery ill! Our lives, to Sa-tan, how en-slaved, How ob-sti-nate our will!

lines: Alas! by nature how depraved,
How prone to every ill!
Our lives, to Satan, how enslaved,
How obstinate our will!
And can such sinners be restored,
Such rebels reconciled?
Can grace itself the means afford
To make a foe a child?
Yes, grace has found the wondrous means
Which shall effectual prove;
To cleanse us from our countless sins,
And teach our hearts to love.
Jesus for sinners undertakes,
And died that we may live;
His blood a full atonement makes,
And cries aloud, "Forgive."
Yet one thing more must grace provide,
To bring us home to God;
Or we shall slight the Lord, who died,
And trample on his blood.
The holy Spirit must reveal
The Savior's work and worth;
Then the hard heart begins to feel
A new and heavenly birth.
Thus bought with blood, and born again,
Redeemed, and saved, by grace
Rebels, in God's own house obtain
A son's and daughter's place.

source: John Newton and William Cowper, Olney Hymns (1779)
licence: Public domain: John Newton died in 1807.
credits: Words by John Newton (1725–1807), public domain, as printed in Olney Hymns (1779); set to ST. AGNES by NoteFusion, as words-only hymn books were sung.
